- [x] I, the PR author, have personally reviewed every line of this PR.

## Why

Separate MFSDP v2 weight release from gradient reduction. Shared layers and delayed weight gradients can finish consuming full weights before parameter-gradient callbacks arrive. Releasing storage at module backward completion avoids retaining those weights while gradient reduction waits for all contributions.

**Depends on #8523.** The diffbase is `pull-request/8523` at `6215df2bd`; its positional layer-input contract and CUDA graph caller changes are inherited. This PR contains the MFSDP lifecycle changes and their regressions. #8113 is already merged.

## Changes

- Register `post_backward()` for module completion and `post_accumulate_grad()` for parameter-gradient completion. Release full weight storage independently of packing and reducing gradients; neither callback waits for the other.
- Keep full-shaped parameter bindings after storage release so delayed `backward_dw()` can assign `.grad`. At final synchronization, `reshard()` restores bindings, releases any remaining storage, and clears unused backward-prefetch events. The frozen-first-layer regression exercises this cleanup across two iterations.
- Update combined 1F1B to use the parameter-gradient completion hook while retaining its explicit resharding. Reject delayed wgrad without caller-managed synchronization.
- Check shared-layer storage lifetime, delayed-wgrad storage release, and TransformerBlock weight release from an input-gradient hook before final autograd cleanup.

Custom modules receiving differentiable inputs only through keywords still use conservative final-callback cleanup, because PyTorch full-backward hooks do not track keyword input gradients. #8523 enforces positional activations for TransformerLayer and MambaLayer.

## Validation

After stacking on #8523, the annotation, context, fully-shard, dense-adapter, and memory suites passed on two RTX A6000 GPUs with NGC 26.08: **73 passed, 10 skipped per rank**. Skips require four or more ranks or Blackwell hardware. Black, Ruff, and `git diff --check` passed.

The two MFSDP production commits replayed without conflicts and have unchanged patches. The existing TransformerBlock storage regression is retained; the older positional-input changes are supplied by #8523.

## Functional performance comparison (NSC-LHR)

The existing GB300 comparison used baseline `dddd756` and PR revision `90cf910`, before the later storage-lifetime changes. These measurements have not been rerun against the current diffbase or head.

Seven existing 8-GPU configurations and one 4-GPU MXFP8 configuration completed **22 training runs of 50 steps**, including repeat comparisons. Every paired logged loss and peak-allocation value matched. Training and optimizer CUDA graph capture completed in the graph recipe.

The runs used `MockGPTDataset` and `NullTokenizer` (50257 tokens), preserving model, batch, and iteration settings. Both benchmark snapshots required the same `caller_managed_grad_sync=True` setup correction in `megatron/training/models/dist_utils.py`. These are paired performance measurements with mock data, not CI corpus/golden-value results.

Step time is the median over iterations 11–50. Memory is the maximum TensorBoard allocation on the CI logging rank, not the maximum across ranks. Each pair ran sequentially in the same allocation and container.

| Configuration | Baseline ms | PR ms | Change | Peak allocated GiB, baseline / PR |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| DeepSeek EP2 | 192.0 | 189.7 | -1.2% | 24.288 / 24.288 |
| DeepSeek EP2 + delayed wgrad | 228.9 | 228.3 | -0.3% | 24.505 / 24.505 |
| Llama-3 proxy + CUDA graphs | 20.8 | 20.6 | -1.0% | 4.183 / 4.183 |
| DeepSeek EP2, two microbatches | 285.2 | 288.1 | +1.0% | 24.290 / 24.290 |
| DeepSeek HSDP, two microbatches | 288.8 | 295.6 | +2.4% | 24.559 / 24.559 |
| DeepSeek HFSDP, two microbatches | 353.5 | 285.4 | -19.3% | 24.360 / 24.360 |
| DeepSeek HFSDP, two microbatches — reverse-order repeat | 311.6 | 311.5 | -0.0% | 24.360 / 24.360 |
| GPT CP2 | 284.2 | 243.9 | -14.2% | 1.247 / 1.247 |
| GPT CP2 — reverse-order repeat | 268.5 | 274.3 | +2.2% | 1.247 / 1.247 |
| DeepSeek MXFP8 (4 GPUs) | 399.3 | 422.8 | +5.9% | 23.199 / 23.199 |
| DeepSeek MXFP8 (4 GPUs) — reverse-order repeat | 402.7 | 402.9 | +0.0% | 23.199 / 23.199 |

The three large initial timing differences did not reproduce in reverse order. Those repeats differ by less than 0.1% for HFSDP/MXFP8 and +2.2% for GPT CP2; the other first-pass differences range from -1.2% to +2.4%. These short runs do not establish a tight throughput bound. Unchanged proxy peak allocation does not rule out the keyword-input retention issue described above.

NSC-LHR jobs: `109746`, `109825`, `109880`, `110026`. Scripts, source archives, training logs, TensorBoard files, and exit-code verification are under `/scratch/fsw/portfolios/coreai/users/jingyuew/mfsdp-functional-7902-20261007` on NSC-LHR.

Contributors can view more details about this message [here](https://docs.gha-runners.nvidia.com/cpr/auto-sync).
I found two issues here: keyword inputs keep all the layer weights in memory during backward, and rebinding a prefetched layer can break its next forward.

Can we track completion for keyword inputs too? TransformerBlock normally calls each layer with hidden_states as a keyword argument, so this defers every layer's weight release until the whole backward finishes. That keeps the full weights for all decoder layers on the stage in memory at once and can make a ZeRO-3 run run out of memory even if it fit before.

This loop then binds its sharded parameters while leaving _unshard_event set, so the next forward skips unsharding and fails with mixed Tensor/DTensor inputs. Running the existing frozen-first-layer test for a second iteration should cover this.

inline_comments.body: Can we keep the parameter binding and _unshard_event in sync here? With a frozen first layer and inputs that don't require gradients, the following trainable layer's backward prefetches the frozen layer, but the frozen layer never runs backward to clear its event. This loop then binds its sharded parameters while leaving _unshard_event set, so the next forward skips unsharding and fails with mixed Tensor/DTensor inputs. Running the existing frozen-first-layer test for a second iteration should cover this.
